blocks.text: The opening conflict concerns particular Pharisees and scribes and their practice of handwashing; it is not a verdict on Jews or Judaism as a whole. Jewish legal and purity reasoning included real disagreements and varied practices, so this chapter should not be used to portray Judaism as uniquely legalistic, hypocritical, or impure.

The immediate accusation is that some disciples eat with unwashed hands, not that they have eaten a prohibited animal. Jesus contrasts what enters the stomach with the harmful thoughts and actions that proceed from the heart. The wording in verse 19 remains disputed: some read it as declaring all foods clean, while others read it as an explanation of digestion that does not settle Torah food distinctions. The passage therefore should not be made into a simple proof either that all Jewish food practice ended or that it has no possible dietary implication. It also keeps bodily impurity, food, and Jewish practice from being treated as moral vice or personal worthlessness.

sections.title: What is at issue in the food discussion?

blocks.text: The woman answers Jesus' saying about children, bread, and dogs by appealing to the crumbs under the table, and her daughter is released. Readers have understood this exchange in differing ways involving testing, boundaries, ethnicity, gender, and possible change; the passage itself reports the exchange and its outcome without resolving all of those questions.

Mark preserves the Semitic word “Ephphatha” and translates it as “Be opened,” drawing attention to Jesus' direct address to the deaf man. The healing story portrays embodied need and restored participation, but it should not be taken to equate disability with sin, weak faith, or spiritual failure, or to stigmatize disabled people through a cure-centered reading.
